"Dal or rajma tonight?"
"Rajma. It's Wednesday."
"Right. Wednesday." Sarita laughed. "Five years and we've turned into a timetable."
"A good timetable," Vijay said, eyes on the cricket score. "Did you pay the electricity bill?"
"Yesterday."
"You're the best."
She set the pressure cooker going. "I went to that pottery class on Saturday, you know. The trial one."
"Hmm? Nice. Was it nice?"
"It was... really nice. I've been thinking about it a lot."
"Good, good." He clapped as someone hit a six. "Oh, did Amma call you about Sunday?"
"She did."
Sarita stirred the rajma and didn't finish the sentence she'd started in her head: that she'd been thinking about more than pottery. About her job, about what she wanted. Vijay was lovely. He just hadn't asked in a long time. And she hadn't pushed.

qa.a: They have rajma because it's Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Sarita thinking about but didn't say?
qa.a: Sarita felt a little lonely, since Vijay hadn't asked in a long time, and had been thinking about more than pottery: her job and what she wants.

qa.q: What small change could help this couple keep knowing each other?
qa.a: Vijay could put the score aside and ask a real follow-up question, and Sarita could say what's on her mind instead of letting it drop.

qa.q: How might Vijay see their evening?
qa.a: Vijay likely sees a happy, easy routine and has no idea Sarita is holding back something important.

grounding: Shows a couple of five years in a warm routine where comfort has replaced curiosity, so a partner's inner changes go unasked and unspoken.

passage:
I'm Lakshmi. Prakash and I have been married four years, and looking back at last year, I can see how comfortable we'd become. Filter coffee at seven, his cycling on Sundays, my mother's call at eight every night. It was easy. I liked easy.
What I didn't notice was how little we asked each other anything real. Prakash stopped mentioning his work around March. I assumed it was fine. My colleague Sangeeta asked once, "How's Prakash's new project?" and I realised I didn't even know he had one.
And I hadn't told him that I'd started dreading my own job. It didn't seem worth bringing up over coffee. We were so busy being comfortable that small changes slipped past, unannounced.
Nothing was wrong. That's what made it so easy to miss.

qa.q: When did Prakash stop mentioning his work?
qa.a: Prakash stopped mentioning his work around March.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi realise when Sangeeta asked about Prakash's project?
qa.a: Lakshmi was surprised to realise they had stopped asking each other about real things, and she didn't even know Prakash had a new project.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi and Prakash do to stay close within their routine?
qa.a: They could keep the comfortable rituals but add a real question now and then, like how work is truly going, and share worries such as Lakshmi's dread before they grow.

qa.q: How might Prakash have been feeling about his new project?
qa.a: Prakash may have been stressed or excited about it but didn't bring it up, perhaps thinking Lakshmi wasn't curious or that it could wait.

grounding: Illustrates a married couple's easy routine in which neither asks about the other's inner life, so changes at work go unspoken.

"Done. Did you call the plumber?"

"Tomorrow. Dal or khichdi tonight?"

"Just tired, Joseph. Work."

"Same."

"...Did you know I've started going to the pottery class on Saturdays?"

"Wait. Since when?"

"Three weeks."

"Three weeks? You never said."

"You never asked where I go on Saturday mornings."

"I thought you were at your mother's."

"I was, the first time."

"Huh. I didn't even notice."

"It's fine. We're fine. It's just... we used to talk about stuff like this."

"We still talk."

"About bills, Joseph. About plumbers."

"...Okay. Tell me about the pottery."

passage:
Samir and I have been together six years. We have a rhythm. I make the coffee, he does the dishes. Sunday is biryani and a film. We finish each other's grocery lists.

I love it. It's safe.

But last month, at a friend's wedding, someone asked Samir what he was reading these days, and he talked for ten minutes about a book on the history of trains. I'd never heard him mention it. I didn't know he liked trains.

On the drive home I asked him, "When did you start that book?"

"Two months ago," he said. "You were busy with your exams."

It wasn't a fight. We laughed about it. But I kept thinking: what else have I stopped asking about? When did the comfort turn into not knowing?

I've started asking him one real question every evening. It feels awkward. It also feels necessary.

— Chetan

qa.q: What book was Samir talking about at the wedding?
qa.a: A book on the history of trains.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel on the drive home?
qa.a: Chetan felt surprised and a little unsettled, realising the comfortable routine had let Chetan stop asking about Samir's inner life.

qa.q: What did Chetan decide to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Chetan started asking Samir one real question every evening, so small changes don't go unspoken inside the comfort.

qa.q: How might Samir feel when Chetan starts asking real questions?
qa.a: He may feel pleased and seen, perhaps a little surprised by the sudden interest.

grounding: Chetan and Samir's comfortable six-year routine is real and safe, but Chetan realises it let them stop asking about each other's inner lives.

Instructor's note, Saturday salsa class

Sahil and Manjula have come every Saturday for a year. They told me they've been together six years. They're easy with each other: she fixes his collar without thinking, he knows exactly when she'll turn.

Today I paired everyone with new partners for one song. Manjula danced with a younger man who asked her questions the whole time: where she grew up, what she likes about dancing. She laughed more in three minutes than I'd seen all year.

Sahil noticed. When they came back together, he asked her, half joking, "What were you two talking about?"

"He asked what I like about salsa," she said. "Nobody's asked me that in a long time."

Sahil looked at her for a second longer than usual. After class, I saw them sitting on the steps, talking, not dancing.

— Ines, instructor

qa.q: What did the younger partner ask Manjula about?
qa.a: Where she grew up and what she likes about dancing.

qa.q: What does Manjula's laughter with the new partner suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed being asked about herself and may feel a little unnoticed in the comfortable routine with Sahil.

qa.q: What small step did Sahil and Manjula take after class?
qa.a: They sat on the steps and talked, a start to asking about each other's inner lives again.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Manjula says no one's asked her that in a long time?
qa.a: He may feel a pang of surprise and guilt, realising he stopped asking.

grounding: A dance instructor's note shows Sahil and Manjula's easy six-year routine and how comfort had let them stop asking about each other's inner lives.

Sunday, 11 p.m.
Five years with Bhupen this winter. Tonight was the usual: khichdi, the cooking show, him on the left of the sofa, me on the right, both scrolling. At ten he said, "Chai, Leela-ji?" in that mock-formal voice, and I said yes without looking up.
It's easy. I love easy.
But today I noticed new running shoes by the door, and I don't know when he started running, or why. And I haven't told him I've been looking at an evening design course; the form has sat open on my laptop for three weeks.
When did we stop asking each other things? We know each other's chai sugar to the grain, and not what the other thinks about on the bus.
Maybe tomorrow I'll ask about the shoes.

qa.a: Leela noticed new running shoes by the door.

qa.q: What does the question 'When did we stop asking each other things?' show about how Leela feels?
qa.a: Leela feels content in the easy routine yet uneasy and a little lonely, noticing that neither knows what the other is quietly thinking about.

qa.a: Asking Bhupen about the running and mentioning the design course over chai would reopen curiosity before more small changes go unspoken.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be experiencing in these easy evenings?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel comfortable but unasked, having started running without it ever coming up, perhaps assuming nobody is curious.
